newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks focus on liability, health.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks focus on liability, health.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

State attorneys general and cigarette makers resumed talks Tuesday to consider several proposals, including one that would limit how much the tobacco industry would pay annually for smokers' injuries.

The attorneys general said they were optimistic about meeting with industry representatives, saying that a Florida jury's verdict in favour of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. in a trial Monday would not affect their negotiations.

"Things look good. We're making progress but it's incremental at this point," Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore said after an early morning session with colleagues, members of the health community and plaintiffs lawyers representing individual smokers.
The negotiators were meeting among themselves in individual groups and with representatives of the tobacco industry throughout the day.
The key issues being discussed were civil liability and public health, including efforts aimed at reducing underage smoking.
Moore said the state lawyers were organised into five working groups to consider separate issues, including whether there is insurance to cover claims against the industry.
The attorneys general have suggested several proposals to the tobacco industry over the past few days on how to deal with the difficult issue of liability.

The states want to give the industry an incentive to settle, but refuse to agree to blanket protection from all lawsuits. The attorneys general have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers.
"Immunity, that word isn't even in our vocabulary," Moore said.
One negotiator told Reuters that one of the proposals would set up a fund with an annual limit, which would allow the industry to know how much to set aside each year.

If a smoker is successful in a lawsuit against the industry and the fund for that year is low, or already has been exhausted, the plaintiff would still get paid, but the full amount might not be received until the following year, the source said.
"This is just one of the proposals. There are other things on the table," he said.
Florida Attorney General Robert Butterworth said the tobacco industry was also looking for a way to eliminate or reduce the possibility of punitive damages.
"I am personally opposed to a cap (on damages). If it is too low, it denies access to the courts," Butterworth said.
Washington Attorney General Christine Gregoire said the parties were not discussing potential criminal actions and no federal authorities or members of congress were involved in the negotiations.
"The only people here are the people that have filed lawsuits," she said.

The U.S. Justice Department is currently investigating the tobacco industry on allegations that include the possibility that manufacturers lied or withheld information from federal agencies about nicotine and addiction and other health risks.
In Jacksonville, Fla., Monday a jury cleared R.J. Reynolds of responsibility for the death of a smoker who died of lung cancer.

The jury deliberated for eight hours over two days before deciding Reynolds had neither acted negligently nor made a dangerous, defective product that caused the death of Jean Connor, who smoked heavily from the time she was a teenager and died of lung cancer in October 1995 at age 49.
Despite the verdict, tobacco company stocks were lower Tuesday after gaining sharply on Monday.

RJR Nabisco Holdings lost $1.75 to $30.875 and Philip Morris was off $1.75 at $42.375, both in heavy trading on the New York Stock Exchange. In contrast, Loews Corp. gained 87.50 cents to $96.50, also on the NYSE.
